blocks.text: Śakuni. Bhīṣma was in search of a suitable bride for the blind prince Dhṛtarāṣṭra. When he heard of Princess Gāndhārī, he sent a messenger to King Subala asking for his daughter's hand in marriage to Dhṛtarāṣṭra. King Ṣubala hesitated at first as Prince Dhṛtarāṣṭra was blind. However, he later agreed considering the greatness of the Kurus and Bhīṣma.

Gāndhārī, on hearing that her parents had arranged her marriage to the blind Dhṛtarāṣṭra, picked up a piece of cloth and blindfolded herself. As her husband was blind, she decided resolutely that she would never experience more than her husband could. Such was her dedication towards her husband that she chose to stand behind him in every sense.

This act of hers has received plentiful praise. But was it the right choice? Modern-day scholars raise a pertinent question, whether the most important thing in a marriage is the evenness of the husband and wife or their compatibility. Shouldn't both partners complement each other as they walk the householder's life?

No matter how much we eulogise her, this hasty Pratijñā certainly has had deep repercussions. Duryodana's stubbornness and inflated ego were never corrected and improper parenting had the lion's share of contribution in the upbringing of some of the most unprincipled characters of the Itihāsa. The choice to keep her eyes closed also has an inner connotation - to turn a blind eye to all the activities done by her sons. Undeniably, the role of the mother is paramount when raising children.
